Memory consolidation is a category of biological processes in the brain that stabilize a memory over time after it is initially learned.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) A memory trace is the biological change in neural circuits caused by acquisition of new information. Consolidation is distinguished into two specific processes. The first, synaptic consolidation, which is thought to correspond to [late-phase long-term potentiation](/wiki/Long-term_potentiation#Late_phase),[[2]](#cite_note-Bramham_2005-2) occurs on a small scale in the synaptic connections and neural circuits within the first few hours after learning. The second process is systems consolidation, occurring on a much larger scale in the brain, with gradual reorganization and reduced reliance on the hippocampus and strengthening of distributed cortical networks over a period of weeks to years. This involves several mechanisms including molecular, synaptic, and systems-level processes that stabilize the [neural ensemble](/wiki/Neuronal_ensemble) ([engram](/wiki/Engram_(neuropsychology))) that is thought to represent the newly formed memory.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Recently, a third process has become the focus of research, reconsolidation, in which previously consolidated memories can be made [labile](/wiki/Lability) again through reactivation of the memory trace.[[4]](#cite_note-Nader-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Sara-5)

/wiki/File:Memory_consolidation.svgThe line processes to make information memory
Memory consolidation was first referred to in the writings of the renowned [Roman](/wiki/Ancient_Rome) teacher of [rhetoric](/wiki/Rhetoric) [Quintillian](/wiki/Quintillian). He noted the "curious fact... that the interval of a single night will greatly increase the strength of the memory," and presented the possibility that "... the power of recollection .. undergoes a process of ripening and maturing during the time which intervenes." The process of consolidation was later proposed based on clinical data illustrated in 1882 by [Ribot's](/wiki/Th%C3%A9odule-Armand_Ribot) [Law of Regression](/wiki/Law_of_Regression), "progressive destruction advances progressively from the unstable to the stable". This idea was elaborated on by William H. Burnham a few years later in a paper on amnesia integrating findings from experimental psychology and neurology. Coining of the term "consolidation" is credited to the German researchers [Müller](/wiki/Georg_Elias_M%C3%BCller) and Alfons Pilzecker who rediscovered the concept that memory takes time to fixate or undergo "Konsolidierung" in their studies conducted between 1892 and 1900.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) The two proposed the perseveration-consolidation [hypothesis](/wiki/Hypothesis) after they found that new information learned could disrupt information previously learnt if not enough time had passed to allow the old information to be consolidated.[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6) This led to the suggestion that new memories are fragile in nature but as time passes they become solidified.[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6)

/wiki/File:Gray739-emphasizing-hippocampus.pngLateral view of the hippocampus which is located in the medial temporal lobeSystematic studies of [anterograde amnesia](/wiki/Anterograde_amnesia) started to emerge in the 1960s and 1970s. The case of [Henry Molaison](/wiki/Henry_Molaison), formerly known as patient H.M., became a [landmark](/wiki/Landmark) in studies of memory as it relates to [amnesia](/wiki/Amnesia) and the removal of the [hippocampal zone](/wiki/Hippocampus) and sparked massive interest in the study of [brain lesions](/wiki/Lesions) and their effect on memory. After Molaison underwent a [bilateral](/wiki/Bilateral_symmetry) [medial](/wiki/Anatomical_terms_of_location#Left_and_right_(lateral),_and_medial) [temporal lobe](/wiki/Temporal_lobe) [resection](/wiki/Segmental_resection) to alleviate [epileptic symptoms](/wiki/Epilepsy) the patient began to suffer from memory impairments. Molaison lost the ability to encode and consolidate newly learned information leading researchers to conclude the [medial temporal lobe](/wiki/Medial_temporal_lobe) (MTL) was an important [structure](/wiki/Structure) involved in this process.[[7]](#cite_note-ScovilleMilner-7) Molaison also showed signs of [retrograde amnesia](/wiki/Retrograde_amnesia) spanning a period of about three years prior to the [surgery](/wiki/Surgery) suggesting that recently acquired memories of as long as a couple years could remain in the MTL prior to consolidation into other brain areas.[[8]](#cite_note-Milner-8) Research into other patients with resections of the MTL have shown a positive relationship between the degree of memory impairment and the extent of MTL removal which points to a temporal [gradient](/wiki/Gradient) in the consolidating nature of the MTL.[[7]](#cite_note-ScovilleMilner-7)

These studies were accompanied by the creation of animal models of human [amnesia](/wiki/Amnesia) in an effort to identify brain substrates critical for slow consolidation. Meanwhile, [neuropharmacological](/wiki/Neuropsychopharmacology) studies of selected brain areas began to shed light on the [molecules](/wiki/Molecules) possibly responsible for fast consolidation.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) In recent decades, advancements in [cellular](/wiki/Cell_(biology)) preparations, [molecular biology](/wiki/Molecular_biology), and [neurogenetics](/wiki/Neurogenetics) have revolutionized the study of consolidation. Providing additional support is the study of functional brain activity in humans which has revealed that the activity of brain regions changes over time after a new memory is acquired.[[7]](#cite_note-ScovilleMilner-7) This change can occur as quickly as a couple hours after the memory has been [encoded](/wiki/Encoding_(memory)) suggesting that there is a [temporal](/wiki/Time) dimension to the reorganization of the memory as it is represented in the [brain](/wiki/Brain).[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6)

## Synaptic consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=2)]

[Synaptic consolidation](/wiki/Synapse) is one form of memory consolidation seen across all species and long-term memory tasks. [Long-term memory](/wiki/Long-term_memory), when discussed in the context of synaptic consolidation, is conventionally said to be [memory](/wiki/Memory) that lasts for at least 24 hours.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) Synaptic consolidation is achieved faster than systems consolidation (which is assumed to take weeks, months, or even to years to be accomplished[[9]](#cite_note-Dudai_et_al._2015-9)). There is evidence to suggest that synaptic consolidation takes place within minutes to hours of [memory encoding](/wiki/Memory_encoding) or [learning](/wiki/Learning) (shown, for example, in goldfish),[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) and as such it is considered the 'fast' type of consolidation. It is also referred to as 'initial consolidation'.[[10]](#cite_note-Okuda_et_al._2020-10) As soon as six hours after training, memories become impervious to interferences that disrupt synaptic consolidation and the formation of long-term memory. [Late-phase LTP](/wiki/Long-term_potentiation#Late_phase),[[2]](#cite_note-Bramham_2005-2) the long-lasting form of one of the best understood forms of [synaptic plasticity](/wiki/Synaptic_plasticity), is thought to be the cellular process underlying synaptic consolidation.

The standard model of synaptic consolidation suggests that alterations of synaptic [protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis) and resulting changes in [membrane potential](/wiki/Membrane_potential) are achieved through activating [intracellular transduction cascades](/wiki/Signal_transduction). These molecular cascades trigger [transcription factors](/wiki/Transcription_factors) that lead to changes in [gene expression](/wiki/Gene_expression). The result of the gene expression is the lasting alteration of synaptic proteins, as well as synaptic remodeling and growth. In a short time-frame immediately following learning, the molecular cascade, expression and process of both transcription factors and [immediate early genes](/wiki/Immediate_early_genes), are susceptible to disruptions. Disruptions caused by specific drugs, antibodies and gross physical trauma can block the effects of synaptic consolidation.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1)

### Synaptic Plasticity
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=4)]

Additionally, synaptic consolidation is supported by multiple forms of [synaptic plasticity](/wiki/Synaptic_plasticity). Synaptic plasticity is largely defined as the ability of a neural connection to change in strength over time due to exposure to different levels of stimuli.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In other words, an organism's neural connections can adapt and change to accommodate different environmental stimuli which can have larger systemic effects. Some mechanistic examples of this include [long-term potentiation](/wiki/Long-term_potentiation) and [long-term depression](/wiki/Long-term_depression).[[12]](#cite_note-12) Long-term potentiation is an increase in the strength of a synaptic input as a result of repeated high-frequency stimulation.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In other words, neural responses across two neurons strengthen over time the more those neurons fire. In contrast to long-term potentiation is long-term depression, which results from low-frequency or lack of stimulation. In conjunction, this means that synaptic connections between neurons can either increase or decrease in strength due to frequency or intensity of use. Global implications of this can be found in brain areas such as the [hippocampus](/wiki/Hippocampus), where one study on rabbits demonstrated that repeated stimulation of hippocampal neurons led to an increase in the future efficacy of their activation.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

### Long-term potentiation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=5)]

LTP can be thought of as the prolonged strengthening of [synaptic transmission](/wiki/Synaptic_transmission),[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) and is known to produce increases in the [neurotransmitter](/wiki/Neurotransmitter) production and [receptor](/wiki/Receptor_(biochemistry)) sensitivity, lasting minutes to even days. The process of [LTP](/wiki/Long-term_potentiation) is regarded as a contributing factor to [synaptic plasticity](/wiki/Synaptic_plasticity) and in the growth of [synaptic strength](/wiki/Synaptic_strength), which are suggested to underlie memory formation. LTP is also considered to be an important mechanism in terms of maintaining memories within brain regions,[[16]](#cite_note-Spencer-16) and therefore is thought to be involved in learning.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) There is compelling evidence that LTP is critical for Pavlovian fear conditioning in rats suggesting that it mediates [learning](/wiki/Learning) and [memory](/wiki/Memory) in mammals. Specifically, [NMDA-receptor](/wiki/NMDA-receptor) [antagonists](/wiki/Receptor_antagonist) appear to block the induction of both LTP and [fear conditioning](/wiki/Fear_conditioning) and that fear conditioning increases [amygdaloidal](/wiki/Amygdala) synaptic transmission that would result in LTP.[[17]](#cite_note-Maren-17)

### Structural Plasticity
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=6)]

In order to discuss how memory consolidation works on a broader scale we have to also acknowledge the broader mechanisms of plasticity that occur outside of the synapse. This brings us to the process of [structural plasticity](/wiki/Structural_plasticity). Structural plasticity represents changes in the broader cell, encompassing both changes in neuron shape, changes in supporting cell shape, and formation of new cells entirely.[[18]](#cite_note-18) Because memory consolidation involves the long-term stabilization of [neural circuits](/wiki/Neural_circuit), these large-scale structural changes are thought to contribute to the persistence and organization of consolidated memories.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The following is a brief list of some of the most significant mechanisms of plasticity in the brain.

[Neurogenesis](/wiki/Neurogenesis) which is the brains process of making new neurons. While this has not been demonstrable in adult humans[[20]](#cite_note-20), neurogenesis is a major contributor to brain plasticity in other organisms such as rodents.[[21]](#cite_note-21) However, it has been proposed that newly generated neurons in the hippocampus can integrate into memory-related circuits in newborns, and this process has been proposed to support certain forms of memory consolidation—particularly those involving pattern separation or long-term retention.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

#### Synaptic Remodelling
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=8)]

However, this is not the only possible mechanism that enables structural changes in neurons. [Dendritic spine](/wiki/Dendritic_spine) remodelling is one of the primary mechanisms by which neuroplasticity is derived. Dendritic spines are signal receiving locations on neurons found on [dendrites](/wiki/Dendrite). There are many types of spines that possess different functions, however the important aspect of them is that their shape and frequency is flexible. Furthermore, there seems to be a direct connection between changes in spines and experiences in rodents,[[23]](#cite_note-23) and dendritic spine remodelling has been established as a significant component in learning and memory.[[24]](#cite_note-24) Because memory consolidation requires the stabilization of experience-dependent synaptic changes, long-term alterations in spine number, size, or morphology are thought to provide a structural substrate for the maintenance of consolidated memories.[[25]](#cite_note-25) This is important as it indicates a direct relationship between experiences and neurological changes. Additionally, spine concentration on a neuron is subject to fluctuation, with that fluctuation relating to regularity of activation. Studies suggest that increased activation of neurons can lead to increases in formation of spines, while over activation can cause loss of them.[[26]](#cite_note-26) This fluidity in spine density provides a further mechanism for neurons to adapt in sensitivity. In summary, due to the combined characteristics of high flexibility of structure and function, as well as the ability to fluctuate in concentration, dendritic spines, via dendritic spine remodelling provides an immense amount of flexibility in the brain. These spine-level changes are believed to play a key role in converting transient synaptic modifications into long-lasting memory traces.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In addition to the aforementioned processes are [synaptogenesis](/wiki/Synaptogenesis) and [synaptic pruning](/wiki/Synaptic_pruning). Synaptogenesis is the process by which a two neurons form a new synapse,[[28]](#cite_note-28) and synaptic pruning is the process by which a synaptic connection between two neurons is eliminated.[[29]](#cite_note-29) In short, these two mechanisms allow for changes in neural connections, facilitating processes of connection formation and connection degradation. This allows for a high level of variability in neural pathways as they can be subject to change based on different conditions. By acting as a mechanism that mediates overall synaptic changes, synaptogenesis and pruning can modify how information is routed and stored over time, thereby influencing the long-term consolidation of memories.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

The last major mechanism of structural plasticity is [myelination](/wiki/Myelination). In the brain, [myelin](/wiki/Myelin) operates as a sheath around neurons increasing the rate at which they transmit signals to each other. This is essential as myelin facilitates rapid processing in necessary neural systems. Myelination is the process with which neurons are wrapped by myelin. Recent research has uncovered that this process of myelination can occur throughout the lifetime of an organism.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Additionally, [oligodendrocytes](/wiki/Oligodendrocyte), which are the cells that comprise myelin in the brain are particularly flexible in their functions even in adults.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Current studies have established that myelin has a high rate of change in the brain, allowing the brain to optimize functioning speeds based on particular needs.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Additionally, it has also been observed that [white matter](/wiki/White_matter) increases can occur in tandem with skill acquisition[[34]](#cite_note-34) or cognitive processing.[[35]](#cite_note-35) This remains consistent with the previous points as white matter is primarily composed of myelin.[[36]](#cite_note-36) Thus, the rapid changes in white matter associated with learning or cognition are a result of rapid changes in myelination. Systems-level memory consolidation depends on coordinated communication across multiple brain regions, thus, activity-dependent changes in myelination are thought to improve the timing and efficiency of these networks, contributing to some of the long-term stabilization of memories.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)

[Distributed learning](/wiki/Distributed_learning) has been found to enhance memory consolidation, specifically for relational memory. Experimental results suggest that distributing learning over the course of 24 hours decreases the rate of forgetting compared to [massed learning](/wiki/Spacing_effect), and enhances relational memory consolidation. When interpreted in the context of synaptic consolidation, mechanisms of synaptic strengthening may depend on the spacing of memory reactivation to allow sufficient time for [protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis) to occur, and thereby strengthen long-term memory.[[39]](#cite_note-Litman-39)

One study that demonstrates this effect was conducted in 1984 by Smith and Rothkopf.[[40]](#cite_note-Smith_Rothkopf_1984_pp._341–358-40) In this experiment, subjects were sorted into three groups to test retention and learning. "Each group was taught the same 8 hour statistics class, but one group was taught the class in one day, the next over the course of four days in one room, and the last was taught the class over the course of four days in different rooms. The subjects were tested five days later in a completely new setting. The results of the experiment were that taking the class over a period of four days was much more effective than taking it in one single mass. Interestingly, the group that took the course over four days and in different rooms performed the best in the final retention test out of all the groups."[[40]](#cite_note-Smith_Rothkopf_1984_pp._341–358-40) This shows that spacing out study sessions and studying in different environments helps with retention as it provides time for the brain to consolidate the information without being interrupted by new information. The benefits of spacing were also demonstrated in an earlier study by Reder and Anderson (1982) which yielded similar results, confirming the spacing effect's relevance and effects on learning.[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-Goldstein_2014-42)

[Protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis) plays an important role in the formation of new [memories](/wiki/Memories). Studies have shown that [protein synthesis inhibitors](/wiki/Protein_synthesis_inhibitor) administered after [learning](/wiki/Learning), weaken memory, suggesting that protein synthesis is required for memory consolidation. Additionally, reports have suggested that the effects of protein synthesis inhibitors also inhibit [LTP](/wiki/Long-term_potentiation).[[43]](#cite_note-Gold-43) However, other results have shown that protein synthesis may not in fact be necessary for memory consolidation, as it has been found that the formation of memories can withstand vast amounts of [protein synthesis inhibition](/wiki/Protein_synthesis_inhibitor), suggesting that this criterion of protein synthesis as necessary for memory consolidation is not unconditional.[[43]](#cite_note-Gold-43)

## Systems consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=12)]

Systems consolidation is the second form of [memory](/wiki/Memory) consolidation. It is a reorganization process in which memories from the [hippocampal](/wiki/Hippocampal) region, where memories are first [encoded](/wiki/Encoding_(memory)), are moved to the [neo-cortex](/wiki/Neo-cortex) in a more permanent form of storage.[[9]](#cite_note-Dudai_et_al._2015-9)[[44]](#cite_note-Roediger-44) Systems consolidation is a slow dynamic process that can take anywhere from one to two decades to be fully formed in humans, unlike synaptic consolidation that only takes minutes to hours for new information to stabilize into memories.[[44]](#cite_note-Roediger-44)

The standard model of systems consolidation has been summarized by Squire and Alvarez (1995);[[45]](#cite_note-Squire_1995-45) it states that when novel information is originally [encoded](/wiki/Encoding_(memory)) and registered, memory of these new [stimuli](/wiki/Stimulus_(physiology)) becomes retained in both the [hippocampus](/wiki/Hippocampus) and [cortical](/wiki/Cerebral_cortex) regions.[[46]](#cite_note-Frankland-46) Later the hippocampus' representations of this information become active in [explicit](/wiki/Explicit_memory) (conscious) recall or [implicit](/wiki/Implicit_memory) (unconscious) recall like in [sleep](/wiki/Sleep) and 'offline' processes.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1)

Memory is retained in the [hippocampus](/wiki/Hippocampus) for up to one week after initial [learning](/wiki/Learning), representing the hippocampus-dependent stage.[[46]](#cite_note-Frankland-46) During this stage the hippocampus is 'teaching' the cortex more and more about the information and when the information is recalled it strengthens the cortico-cortical connection thus making the memory hippocampus-independent.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) Therefore, from one week and beyond the initial [training](/wiki/Training) experience, the memory is slowly transferred to the [neo-cortex](/wiki/Neo-cortex) where it becomes permanently stored.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1) In this view the hippocampus can perform the task of storing memories temporarily because the synapses are able to change quickly whereas the neocortical synapses change over time.[[45]](#cite_note-Squire_1995-45) Consolidation is thus the process whereby the hippocampus activates the neocortex continually leading to strong connections between the two. Since the hippocampus can only support memories temporarily the remaining activation will be seen only in the neocortex which is able to support memory indefinitely. Squire and Alvarez took the temporally graded nature of patients with retrograde amnesia as support for the notion that once a connection has been established within the neocortex the hippocampus is no longer required, but this process is dynamic and extends for several years.

Squire and Alvarez also proposed the idea that MTL structures play a role in the consolidation of memories within the neocortex by providing a [binding](/wiki/Binding_problem) area for multiple [cortical](/wiki/Cerebral_cortex) [regions](/wiki/Regions) involved in the initial encoding of the memory.[[45]](#cite_note-Squire_1995-45) In this sense the MTL would act as a relay station for the various perceptual input that make up a memory and stores it as a whole event. After this has occurred the MTL directs information towards the neocortex to provide a permanent representation of the memory.

### Multiple trace theory
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=14)]

Multiple trace theory (MTT) builds on the distinction between [semantic memory](/wiki/Semantic_memory) and [episodic memory](/wiki/Episodic_memory) and addresses perceived shortcomings of the standard model with respect to the dependency of the hippocampus. MTT argues that the hippocampus is always involved in the retrieval and storage of episodic memories.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) It is thought that semantic memories, including basic information encoded during the storage of episodic memories, can be established in structures apart from the hippocampal system such as the neo-cortex in the process of consolidation.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) Hence, while proper hippocampal functioning is necessary for the retention and retrieval of episodic memories, it is less necessary during the encoding and use of semantic memories. As memories age there are long-term interactions between the hippocampus and neo-cortex and this leads to the establishment of aspects of memory within structures aside from the hippocampus.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) MTT thus states that both episodic and semantic memories rely on the hippocampus and the latter becomes somewhat independent of the hippocampus during consolidation.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47)
An important distinction between MTT and the standard model is that the standard model proposes that all memories become independent of the hippocampus after several years. However, Nadel and Moscovitch have shown that the hippocampus was involved in memory recall for all remote [autobiographical](/wiki/Autobiographical) memories no matter of their age.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) An important point they make while interpreting the results is that activation in the hippocampus was equally as strong regardless of the fact that the memories recalled were as old as 45 years prior to the date of the experiment.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) This is complicated by the fact that the hippocampus is constantly involved in the encoding of new events and activation due to this fact is hard to separate using baseline measures.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) Because of this, activation of the hippocampus during retrieval of distant memories may simply be a [by-product](/wiki/By-product) of the subject encoding the study as an event.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47)

Haist, Gore, and Mao, sought to examine the temporal nature of consolidation within the hippocampus to test MTT against the standard view.[[48]](#cite_note-Haist-48) They found that the hippocampus does not substantially contribute to the recollection of remote memories after a period of a few years. They claim that advances in the functional magnetic resonance imaging have allowed them to improve their distinction between the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex which they claim is more enduring in its activation from remote memory retrieval.[[48]](#cite_note-Haist-48) They also criticize the use of memories during testing which cannot be confirmed as accurate.[[48]](#cite_note-Haist-48) Finally, they state that the initial interview in the scanner acted as an encoding event as such differences between recent and remote memories would be obscured.[[48]](#cite_note-Haist-48)

### Semantic vs. episodic memory
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=16)]

Nadel and Moscovitch argued that when studying the structures and systems involved in [memory](/wiki/Memory) consolidation, [semantic memory](/wiki/Semantic_memory) and [episodic memory](/wiki/Episodic_memory) need to be distinguished as relying on two different memory systems. When episodic information is encoded there are semantic aspects of the memory that are encoded as well and this is proposed as an explanation of the varying gradients of memory loss seen in amnesic patients.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) Amnesic patients with hippocampal damage show traces of memories and this has been used as support for the standard model because it suggests that memories are retained apart from the hippocampal system.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) Nadel and Moscovitch argue that these retained memories have lost the richness of experience and exist as depersonalized events that have been semanticized over time.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47) They suggest that this instead provides support for their notion that episodic memories rely significantly on the hippocampal system but semantic memories can be established elsewhere in the brain and survive hippocampal damage.[[47]](#cite_note-NadelMoscovitch-47)

### Declarative vs. procedural knowledge consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=17)]

Learning can be distinguished by two forms of knowledge: [declarative](/wiki/Declarative_memory) and [procedural](/wiki/Procedural_memory). Declarative information includes the [conscious](/wiki/Conscious) recall of facts, episodes, and lists, and its storage typically connected with the mediotemporal lobe and the hippocampal systems as it includes the encoding of both semantic and episodic information of events. [Procedural knowledge](/wiki/Procedural_knowledge) however has been said to function separate from this system as it relies primarily on motor areas of the brain.[[49]](#cite_note-Squire-49) The implicit nature of procedural knowledge allows it to exist absent from the conscious awareness that the information is there. Amnesic patients have shown retained ability to be trained on tasks and exhibit learning without the subject being aware that the training had ever taken place.[[49]](#cite_note-Squire-49) This introduces a dissociation between the two forms of memory and the fact that one form can exist absent the other suggests separate mechanisms are involved in consolidation. Squire has proposed the procedural knowledge is consolidated in some cases by the extrapyramidal motor system.[[49]](#cite_note-Squire-49) Squire demonstrated that intact learning of certain motor, perceptual, and cognitive skills can be retained in patients with amnesia.[[49]](#cite_note-Squire-49) They also retain the ability to be influenced by priming effects without the patients being able to consciously recall any training session occurring.[[49]](#cite_note-Squire-49)

### Emotional and stressful memory consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=18)]

The [amygdala](/wiki/Amygdala), specifically the [basolateral region](/wiki/Basolateral_amygdala) (BLA) is involved in the encoding of significant experiences and has been directly linked to memorable events.[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6) Extensive evidence suggests that stress hormones such as epinephrine play a critical role in consolidating new memories and this is why stressful memories are recalled vividly.[[50]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh2-50) Studies by Gold and van Buskirk provided initial evidence for this relationship when they showed that injections of epinephrine into subjects following a training period resulted in greater long-term retention of task related memories.[[51]](#cite_note-GoldVanBuskirk-51)[[52]](#cite_note-Gold2-52) This study also provided evidence that the level of epinephrine injected was related to the level of retention suggesting that the level of stress or emotionality of the memory plays a role on the level of retention. It is suggested that epinephrine affects memory consolidation by activating the amygdala and studies have shown that [antagonism](/wiki/Antagonist) of [beta-andrenoreceptors](/wiki/Adrenergic_receptor) prior to [injection](/wiki/Injection_(medicine)) of [epinephrine](/wiki/Epinephrine) will block the retention of memory effects seen previously.[[53]](#cite_note-Liang-53)[[54]](#cite_note-Liang2-54) This is supported by the fact that beta-adrenoreceptor [agonists](/wiki/Agonists) have the opposite effect on the enhancement of memory consolidation.[[53]](#cite_note-Liang-53)[[54]](#cite_note-Liang2-54) The BLA is thought to be actively involved in memory consolidation and is influenced strongly by stress hormones resulting in increased activation and as such increased memory retention.[[50]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh2-50) The BLA then projects to the hippocampus resulting in a strengthened memory.[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6) This relationship was studied by Packard and Chen who found that when [glutamate](/wiki/Glutamate) was administered to the hippocampus, enhanced consolidation was seen during food-rewarded maze tasks.[[55]](#cite_note-Packard-55) The opposite effect was also seen when the amygdala was inactivated using [lidocaine](/wiki/Lidocaine).[[55]](#cite_note-Packard-55) Studies appear to suggest that the amygdala effects the consolidation of memories through its influence with stress hormones and the projections to other brain areas implicated in memory consolidation.[[6]](#cite_note-JamesLMcGaugh-6)

### Sleep consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=19)]

During sleep, newly encoded memories are stabilized and reorganized with the help of the interactions between the neocortex and the hippocampus. [[56]](#cite_note-56)

Early research focused on [Rapid eye movement](/wiki/Rem_sleep) (REM) [sleep](/wiki/Sleep) as a key important stage for memory consolidation by establishing information in the [hippocampal](/wiki/Hippocampal) and [cortical](/wiki/Cerebral_cortex) regions of the [brain](/wiki/Human_brain).[[57]](#cite_note-Walker-57) REM sleep elicits an increase in [neuronal](/wiki/Neuronal) activity following an enriched or novel waking experience, thus increasing neuronal plasticity and therefore playing an essential role in the consolidation of memories.[[58]](#cite_note-Riberio-58) This has come into question in recent years however and studies on [sleep deprivation](/wiki/Sleep_deprivation) have shown that animals and humans who are denied REM sleep do not show deficits in task learning. It has been proposed that since the brain is in a non-memory encoding state during sleep, consolidation would be unlikely to occur.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59)

More recent studies, however, have suggested slow-wave sleep plays a central role on memory consolidation rather than REM sleep. A review on sleep related memory consolidation methods looked into a combination of the coordination between thalamocortical sleep spindles, hippocampal sharp-wave ripples and cortical slow oscillations to explain the transfer of new memories from the Hippocampus to neocortical networks supporting long-term memory stabilization.[[60]](#cite_note-60) One study found that low levels of acetylcholine found in the central nervous system, which are present during slow-wave sleep, aid in the consolidation of memories and therefore assist in the learning process.[[61]](#cite_note-Gais_Hüllemann_Hallschmid_Born_2006_pp._786–791-61)[[62]](#cite_note-62)

Recent studies have examined the relationship between REM sleep and procedural learning consolidation.
In particular studies have been done on [sensory](/wiki/Sensory_perception) and [motor](/wiki/Motor_skill) related tasks. In one study testing finger-tapping, people were split into two groups and tested post-training with or without intervening sleep; results concluded that sleep post-training increases both speed and accuracy in this particular task, while increasing the activation of both cortical and [hippocampal](/wiki/Hippocampal) regions; whereas the post-training awake group had no such improvements.[[57]](#cite_note-Walker-57) It has been theorized that this may be related more-so to a process of synaptic consolidation rather than systems consolidation because of the short-term nature of the process involved.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59) Researchers examining the effect of sleep on motor learning have noted that while consolidation occurs over a period of 4–6 hours during sleep, this is also true during waking hours, which may negate any role of sleep in learning.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59) In this sense sleep would serve no special purpose to enhance consolidation of memories because it occurs independently of sleep.
Other studies have examined the process of replay which has been described as a reactivation of patterns that were stimulated during a learning phase. Replay has been demonstrated in the hippocampus and this has lent support to the notion that it serves a consolidation purpose.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59) However, replay is not specific to sleep and both rats and primates show signs during restful-awake periods.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59) Also, replay may simply be residual activation in areas that were involved previously in the learning phase and may have no actual effect on consolidation.[[59]](#cite_note-Vertes-59) This reactivation of the memory traces has also been seen in non-REM sleep specifically for hippocampus-dependent memories.[[63]](#cite_note-Wamsley-63) New evidence further suggests that REM sleep contributes to memory consolidation by facilitating selective reactivation of memory traces, which can either strengthen or weaken them.[[64]](#cite_note-64) Researchers have also noted strong reactivation of the hippocampus during sleep immediately after a learning task. This reactivation led to enhanced performance on the learned task.[[63]](#cite_note-Wamsley-63) One such experiment had participants learn word pair associations (declarative memories) before either retention periods of sleep or periods of wakefulness. Researchers found that retrieval expectancy played a role as to whether participants were able to retain the information, as the participants that had been told about the delayed retrieval test performed better. However, their research showed that sleep was more likely to benefit the consolidation of memories if the information was relevant to future events or behaviors.[[65]](#cite_note-65) Researchers following this line of work have come to assume that [dreams](/wiki/Dream) are a by-product of the reactivation of the brain areas and this can explain why dreams may be unrelated to the information being consolidated.[[63]](#cite_note-Wamsley-63) The dream experience itself is not what enhances memory performance but rather it is the reactivation of the neural circuits that causes this. Other researchers have looked at the role growth hormones play in the consolidation of memories, particularly those of procedural and declarative memories. They found that although growth hormones support general brain systems and memory functioning, it is still unclear if growth hormones play a role in the formation and processing of particular memories during sleep periods.[[61]](#cite_note-Gais_Hüllemann_Hallschmid_Born_2006_pp._786–791-61)

#### Cortical slow oscillation- and spindle-complexes
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=20)]

Memory consolidation during sleep via reactivation of prior experiences and information is associated with sleep signatures of cortical "slow [oscillations](/wiki/Neural_oscillation)" and [sleep spindles](/wiki/Sleep_spindle) that are involved in the information flow between relevant brain areas. These oscillatory events coordinate the timing of these interactions in order to facilitate the transfer of information from the hippocampus to the neocortex.[[66]](#cite_note-66) A more complete understanding of these mechanics may possibly allow purposely enabling or strengthening this reactivation.[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)

#### Zif268 and REM sleep
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=21)]

[Zif268](/wiki/Zif268) is an [immediate early gene](/wiki/Immediate_early_gene) (IEG) thought to be involved in neuroplasticity by an [up-regulation](/wiki/Up-regulation) of the transcription factor during [REM sleep](/wiki/REM_sleep) after pre-exposure to an enriched environment.[[58]](#cite_note-Riberio-58) Results from studies testing the effects of zif268 on mice brains [postmortem](/wiki/Postmortem), suggest that a waking experience prior to sleep can have an enduring effect in the brain, due to an increase of neuroplasticity.[[58]](#cite_note-Riberio-58)

Memory reconsolidation is the process of previously consolidated memories being recalled and actively consolidated.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) It is a distinct process that serves to maintain, strengthen and modify [memories](/wiki/Memories) that are already stored in the [long-term memory](/wiki/Long-term_memory). Once memories undergo the process of consolidation and become part of long-term memory, they are thought of as stable. However, the retrieval of a [memory trace](/wiki/Memory_trace) can cause another [labile](/wiki/Labile) phase that then requires an active process to make the [memory](/wiki/Memory) stable after retrieval is complete.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) It is believed that post-retrieval stabilization is different and distinct from consolidation, despite its overlap in function (e.g. [storage](/wiki/Storage_(memory))) and its mechanisms (e.g. [protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis)). Memory modification needs to be demonstrated in the retrieval in order for this independent process to be valid.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15)

The theory of reconsolidation has been debated for many years and is still controversial. Reconsolidation was first conceptualized in light of the discovery that [phobias](/wiki/Phobias) could often be eliminated by means of [electroconvulsive shock therapy](/wiki/Electroconvulsive_shock_therapy) (ECT).[[69]](#cite_note-69) This seemed to indicate the involvement of a re-consolidation process for excited memories, and that the operation active in ECT was the disruption of that process; here, of the reconsolidation of retrieved fear memories by shock administration.

Further studies investigated the concept,[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) using ECT to test for reconsolidation; ECT was already known as an [amnesic](/wiki/Amnesic) agent (leads to memory loss). These studies found it to be effective on retrieved memories when administered directly after the retrieval of a memory.[[1]](#cite_note-Dudai-1)

Later research, wherein fear memories had been established in rats through [Pavlovian](/wiki/Pavlovian) [fear conditioning](/wiki/Fear_conditioning), found that a consolidated fear memory can be brought to a [labile](/wiki/Labile) state, by means of immediate [amygdala](/wiki/Amygdala) infusions of the [protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis) inhibitor [anisomycin](/wiki/Anisomycin), but not by infusions made six hours afterwards.[[4]](#cite_note-Nader-4) It was concluded that consolidated fear memory, when reactivated, enters a changeable state that requires de novo [protein synthesis](/wiki/Protein_synthesis) for new consolidation, i.e., re-consolidation of the old memory.[[4]](#cite_note-Nader-4) Nader, Schafe, and Le Doux (2000) demonstrated that the reconsolidation process may make memories more malleable than previously believed.[[70]](#cite_note-70)[[42]](#cite_note-Goldstein_2014-42) Nader and his colleagues trained rats to be afraid of a tone by pairing the tone with a small shock. Groups of rats were then injected with anisomycin, an antibiotic that restricts protein synthesis, at different points in time. The rats that were injected with anisomycin after consolidation had taken place, retained the fear reaction to the tone. However, the rats that were injected before consolidation and reconsolidation could take place, did not retain the fear response when they heard the tone again later. It seems that interference that is made before memories are consolidated affect the way they are remembered later.

Brunet and colleagues (2008) studied patients that had been diagnosed with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder ([PTSD](/wiki/Posttraumatic_stress_disorder)).[[71]](#cite_note-71) Following the same method that Nader and his associates used, Brunet induced anxiety responses in the patients by having them listen to a 30 second recording describing the circumstances of their traumatic experiences. The patients were shortly thereafter injected with propranolol, a drug that blocks stress hormone receptors in the amygdala which is implicated in neurologically representing the emotional content of memories. These patients experienced a significant reduction in PTSD symptoms months after treatment. These findings were confirmed in later studies done in 2009 by Kindt and colleagues and in 2010 by Schiller and colleagues.[[72]](#cite_note-:0-72)[[73]](#cite_note-73)

These studies done by Nader and others seem to suggest that as memories are being remembered, they are fragile, as if experiencing them for the first time.

In addition to fear memories, appetitive memories are also prone to reconsolidation episodes, which can likewise be disrupted; namely, after local administration of a protein activity inhibitor.[[74]](#cite_note-drug_memory-74)

Since those breakthrough studies were done, there have been several others to probe the theory of memory reconsolidation. Subjects in these studies, along with [humans](/wiki/Human), have included [crabs](/wiki/Crabs), [chicks](/wiki/Chicken), [honeybees](/wiki/Honeybees), [medaka fish](/wiki/Oryzias_latipes), [lymnaea](/wiki/Lymnaea), and various [rodents](/wiki/Rodents).[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) Further studies have demonstrated an analogue of memory reconsolidation in spinal cord pain processing pathways, suggesting a general role for reconsolidation in the [central nervous system](/wiki/Central_nervous_system).[[75]](#cite_note-pain_reconsolidation-75)

Some studies have supported this theory, while others have failed to demonstrate disruption of consolidated memory after retrieval. Negative results may be examples of conditions where memories are not susceptible to a permanent disruption, thus a determining factor of reconsolidation.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) After much debate and a detailed review of this field it had been concluded that reconsolidation was a real phenomenon.[[5]](#cite_note-Sara-5) Tronson and Taylor compiled a lengthy summary of multiple reconsolidation studies, noting a number of studies were unable to show memory impairments due to blocked reconsolidation. However the need for standardized methods was underscored as in some learning tasks such as [fear conditioning](/wiki/Fear_conditioning), certain forms of memory reactivation could actually represent new [extinction](/wiki/Extinction_(psychology)) [learning](/wiki/Learning) rather than activation of an old [memory trace](/wiki/Memory_trace). Under this possibility, traditional disruptions of reconsolidation might actually maintain the original memory trace but prevent the consolidation of [extinction](/wiki/Extinction_(psychology)) [learning](/wiki/Learning).[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) Recent work has suggested that [epigenetic](/wiki/Epigenetics) modifications may also prevent reconsolidation in some cases.[[76]](#cite_note-HDAC-76) The removal of these epigenetic modifications with inhibitors of [histone deacetylase](/wiki/Histone_deacetylase) enabled the erasure of remote memories after recall.

Reconsolidation [experiments](/wiki/Experiment) are more difficult to run than typical consolidation experiments as disruption of a previously consolidated memory must be shown to be specific to the reactivation of the original [memory trace](/wiki/Memory_trace). Furthermore, it is important to demonstrate that the [vulnerability](/wiki/Vulnerability) of reactivation occurs in a limited time frame, which can be assessed by delaying [infusion](/wiki/Infusion_pump) till six hours after reactivation. It is also useful to show that the [behavioral](/wiki/Behavioral) measure used to assess disruption of [memory](/wiki/Memory) is not just due to task impairment caused by the procedure, which can be demonstrated by testing control groups in absence of the original [learning](/wiki/Learning). Finally, it is important to rule out alternative explanations, such as [extinction](/wiki/Extinction_(psychology)) [learning](/wiki/Learning) by lengthening the reactivation phase.[[15]](#cite_note-Tronson-15) There have also been concerns about the use of reconsolidation research to justify psychotherapy treatments, and the generalizability of basic reconsolidation research into the therapy room[[77]](#cite_note-77)

### Distinctions from consolidation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Memory_consolidation&action=edit&section=25)]

Questions arose if reconsolidation was a unique process or merely another phase of consolidation. Both consolidation and reconsolidation can be disrupted by pharmacological agents (e.g. the [protein synthesis](/wiki/Translation_(genetics)) inhibitor [anisomycin](/wiki/Anisomycin)) and both require the [transcription factor](/wiki/Transcription_factor) [CREB](/wiki/CREB). However, recent amygdala research suggests that [BDNF](/wiki/BDNF) is required for consolidation (but not reconsolidation) whereas the [transcription factor](/wiki/Transcription_factor) and [immediate early gene](/wiki/Immediate_early_genes) [Zif268](/wiki/Zif268) is required for reconsolidation but not consolidation.[[78]](#cite_note-78) A similar [double dissociation](/wiki/Double_dissociation) between [Zif268](/wiki/Zif268) for reconsolidation and [BDNF](/wiki/BDNF) for consolid
